title: Jordan Davis trade grades: Eagles kickstart rebuild, Jaguars push for 2026 AFC and Super Bowl titles - CBS Sports
description: Grading how both squads made out in the biggest trade on the eve of the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline
body:
Grading how both squads made out in the biggest trade on the eve of the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:26 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Jacksonville Jaguars capped their flurry of activity on the eve of the NFL's 2026 trade deadline with a blockbuster: they traded a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis. Davis was the 13th overall pick in the 2022 NFL Draft out of Georgia and was also a starter on the Eagles' Super Bowl LIX title team in the 2024 season. Jacksonville doesn't have to worry about a long-term contract with Davis since Philadelphia extended Davis on a three-year, $78 million extension this past offseason. On Monday, the Jaguars have relinquished a 2027 first-round pick, a 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 fifth-round pick, a 2028 sixth-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for the services of Davis, Atlanta Falcons Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III and New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.   Meanwhile, the Eagles now have 10 draft picks in the first two rounds of the NFL Draft across the next three years. They have their own first-round pick and second-round pick, plus the Jaguars' first-round pick in 2027. They have their own first-round pick and own second-round pick plus the New England Patriots' first-round pick (A.J. Brown trade) and the Baltimore Ravens' second-round pick (Cam Jurgens trade) in 2028. In 2029, they have their own first-round pick, their own second-round pick and the Jaguars' second-round pick (Jordan Davis trade).So how does each side grade out in Monday evening's blockbuster deal? Let's dive in.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Jacksonville Jaguars: B-The Jaguars are right to go all in for the 2026 season. The Buffalo Bills (6-1) have one of the leakiest secondaries in the NFL, allowing 254.7 passing yards per game (the third-most in the entire NFL). The Denver Broncos (7-2) have offensive inconsistency issues because of quarterback Bo Nix, whose 5.6 air yards per pass attempt is the second-worst among 31 qualified quarterbacks this season. Nix's 5.6 air yards per pass attempt is mere decimal points ahead of Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) quarterback Patrick Mahomes' 5.6 air yards per pass attempt to avoid being dead last in the league. Mahomes' league-worst air yards per pass attempt figure has more to do with the Chiefs' limited passing game options than an unwillingness to throw the ball downfield like Nix.The AFC North-leading Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) have Aaron Rodgers at quarterback, and he will be 43 years old by the time the playoffs begin. Jacksonville beat the Cincinnati Bengals (6-2) in a narrow, one-score game earlier this season, and the New England Patriots (5-4) just got decimated at home (45-27) by quarterback Jordan Love and his Green Bay Packers.Jacksonville's timing is right, but the price they paid for Davis is not. A first-round pick and a second-round pick for Davis isn't all that different from what the Chicago Bears gave up (2027 and 2028 first-round picks plus a 2027 fourth-round pick) for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, the best defensive tackle in football at the moment. Sure, the Jaguars were never going to get Simmons since he was on an AFC South division rival, the Tennessee Titans, but couldn't they have gotten Davis for a slightly cheaper price? The Bears are getting a player whose 17 sacks over the last two seasons are the most in the league among defensive tackles, while Davis has just 9.5 career sacks.
Yes, Davis can be incredibly impactful in the run game just because of his frame (6-feet-6-inches tall while weighing 336 pounds), but one would think that the Jaguars would have been able to acquire a more well-rounded defensive tackle at the price point of a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick. Davis will certainly help Jacksonville, but what they gave up for him was a little rich. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Philadelphia Eagles: AHats off to Eagles general manager Howie Roseman because he's done it again. He recognized that the 2026 season was dead with quarterback Jalen Hurts (blood clots) sidelined, and the team was on a seven-game losing streak, putting their record at 2-7 through nine games. Roseman also extended two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jalen Carter on a four-year, $152 million extension last offseason, and it was clear that Philadelphia likely wouldn't be able to keep both Carter and Davis for years to come in order to have a well-balanced roster. Roseman was able to trade away the lesser player of the two, and he recouped first-round and second-round draft capital in the deal. He couldn't have asked for anything more, and he'll be able to rebuild the Eagles in no time with 10 picks in the first two rounds of the draft across the next three years.

title: Jaguars-Falcons trade grades: Jacksonville acquires All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III to bolster defense - CBS Sports
description: Bates, who is in the final year of his contract, heads to Jacksonville in exchange for two future draft picks
body:
Bates, who is in the final year of his contract, heads to Jacksonville in exchange for two future draft picks
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:39 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On the eve of Tuesday's trade deadline, dominoes are starting to fall across the league with Week 9 largely in the books. And now, the Jaguars have acquired All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III in a trade with the Atlanta Falcons, according to ESPN. As Bates heads to Duval County, the Falcons receive a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick in return. Bates is in the final year of his contract and is set to be a free agent at the end of this season. While this is looked at as a rental, the 29-year-old should prove to be a key addition to Jacksonville's secondary as it looks to make a serious postseason push following a 6-2 start to the regular season. 
In nine games played for the Falcons this season, Bates has recorded one interception, three forced fumbles, and 60 total tackles. The veteran has also allowed a 78.3% completion percentage to go with a 115.2 passer rating in coverage, per TruMedia. Bates entered the NFL as a second-round draft choice of the Bengals in 2018 out of Wake Forest. After spending his first five years of his career in Cincinnati, he inked a four-year, $64.02 million contract with the Falcons in the spring of 2023 and has been lurking in their secondary ever since. 
Bates is tied for the second-most interceptions (28) in the NFL since coming into the league and has been named a second-team All-Pro three times, including in 2025. Atlanta spent last offseason inking several veterans to extensions, including Bijan Robinson and Drake London. Bates was not among them, and after dropping to 3-6 on the season with a loss to the Bengals in Madrid on Sunday, they're electing to move off of the talented safety for future draft capital. Jessie Bates trade grades
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Jaguars: BJacksonville gave up quite a bit to land Bates. Two picks -- particularly a second-rounder in 2027 -- is a hefty price to pay, especially considering that Bates is set to be a free agent at the end of this season. I do wonder, however, whether that price indicates that Jacksonville views Bates as more than just a rental. After all, the organization does have a history of extending players that they've acquired in midseason trades. For instance, after trading for wideout Jakobi Meyers around last year's deadline, they later signed him to a three-year, $60 million extension. I'll be curious to see if Bates follows a similar path. 
Regardless of whether he's with the Jags for the next few months or years, it's a great move for the 2026 squad. Bates is one of the best safeties in the NFL. In fact, he's the player in the past 40 years with at least 800 tackles and 25 interceptions before age 30. He comes in as a premier piece for the secondary, while also deepening a safety room that has been hit by injuries, most recently losing Eric Murray for the rest of the season to an elbow injury. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Atlanta Falcons: B+Give Atlanta the slight edge here. While they are losing a blue-chip player in their secondary, they were probably going to lose him anyway in free agency later this offseason.The Falcons spent the bulk of last offseason extending key pieces to their core, and that did not include Bates. While the team is technically still in the division race despite a 3-6 record, it doesn't feel like this season will see them making a sizable push if/when they reach the postseason. With that in mind, it's the more prudent move to move off of Bates, get worse in the secondary in the immediate, but collect legit draft capital to position yourself better down the road. 
Getting a second-rounder as part of this deal is nothing to turn your nose up at and is better than any sort of compensatory pick they'd receive if Bates walked in free agency.

        When Ohio State struggles, it quickly becomes national news, and it even bleeds into the political realm. Vice President JD Vance even made light of the Buckeyes' loss to Oregon at a speaking engagement on Monday.Vance was the keynote speaker at a Small Business Administration conference in Washington, and he made sure to poke fun at his alma mater during his opening remarks. Vance, who graduated from Ohio State in 2009, did express optimism that the team would get back on track down the stretch."Before I get into the meat of my remarks, I wanted to talk about the devastating loss last week," Vance said. "There are a lot of people unfairly criticizing the leader of the team despite leading us to a great victory two years ago. ... There's a lot of staff infighting and questions about reshuffling. There's a conversation about whether the No. 2 has what it takes to ultimately lead the team."I'm talking, of course, about the Ohio State Buckeyes. Let me just assure you that I really believe in Luke Fahey, our backup QB, and I think our team is gonna make an amazing turnaround."
Vance was also making a cheeky comparison to last week's midterm election results, in which Republicans lost key races in Vance's home state of Ohio, other battlegrounds and even conservative strongholds like Texas and South Carolina, leading to questions about the leadership and long-term vision of the Republican Party.In Columbus, there has been a shake-up in the wake of the devastating loss. Ryan Day has fired special teams coach Robby Discher, sources told CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz. One of the key turning points on Saturday was Oregon's fake punt, which caught Ohio State off guard and sparked a dramatic rally by the Ducks.
If the Buckeyes are going to turn this around down the stretch, the offense has to improve with Fahey at quarterback because Ohio State finishes with three tricky matchups against Northwestern, Nebraska and Michigan.

        There is always something brewing when Kansas and Kentucky face off, especially considering that Tyran Stokes picked Kansas over Kentucky to end a feverish recruiting battle in April. The potential future No. 1 pick will lace 'em up against a coach in Mark Pope, who spent months trying to woo Stokes to Lexington and drew heat from every corner of BBN when he came up short. It's the story of this game, but Tuesday's Champions Classic is also a golden opportunity for both No. 15 Kansas and No. 24 Kentucky to show that they're far better than their current national status.Let's dive into the nuts and bolts of this blue-blood matchup, starting with projected starting lineups:Kentucky: G Zoom Diallo, G Alex Wilkins, F Milan Momcilovic, F Ousmane N'Diaye, C Malachi Moreno
Kansas: G Taylen Kinney, G Tre White, G Tyran Stokes, F Trey Kaufman-Renn, F Keanu Dawes
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Kentucky vs. Kansas: Need to knowAll eyes on Mr. Stokes: Recruiting drama aside, Stokes is also a real matchup problem for Kentucky in this spot. Pope does not have many good options to handle Kansas' 6-8 freshman wing, who is too big for guards and way too fast for most forwards. Sharpshooter Milan Momcilovic is in Lexington to bang 3-pointers, but Kentucky needs him to play the best defensive game of the season. Momcilovic on Stokes is a matchup Kentucky may have to live with, and it's going to be something Kansas coach Bill Self targets from the jump. If Momcilovic can't handle Stokes' bully-ball drives, Kentucky may have to try Zoom Diallo. Maybe redshirt-freshman wing Braydon Hawthorne could also be part of the solution. Hawthorne's got an enormous wingspan and has impressed defensively so far. Stokes is a problem for everybody, but especially this Kentucky roster. If Stokes goes off, Kentucky is in hot water.Mark Pope's big game woes: Kentucky is 29-26 against high-major teams under Pope. That is far from the standard. One common denominator has been a halfcourt offense gone awry. Self is going to do whatever it takes to keep Kentucky from getting free for its patented transition 3-pointers. If you can make this Kentucky team execute in the halfcourt, there are many more outs for Kansas' defense. But that's easier said than done. Kansas' starting lineup has barely played together this season after Kaufman-Renn's late addition to the roster. Kentucky has plenty of shooting and length surrounding a big man in Malachi Moreno who can really pass the basketball. If Kansas' defense is not connected, Kentucky has the offensive personnel to make it pay. 
Melvin Council Jr. broke his foot; what does it mean? Kansas is losing its dawg and its soul. Council is the high-energy sparkplug who is a voracious defender, an all-out competitor and one of the fastest guards in all of college basketball. Kansas will absolutely miss his speed. Self has a decision to make, whether to go big with Keanu Dawes or Christian Reeves to guard Moreno or to stay small and insert Toledo transfer Leroy Blyden Jr., who is quite fast and owns a feathery jumper. That optionality is a good thing. I also think it does just ramp up the usage rate for Stokes and Kaufman-Renn. I'd love to see Stokes and TKR get rolling in the pick-and-roll game together. Those are two giant playmakers who could put Kentucky's defense into some rough positions. They've just barely played together this year, so it's hard to imagine the Stokes-TKR, two-man game humming on all cylinders right away.Where to watch Kentucky vs. Kansas liveDate: Tuesday, Nov. 10 | Time: 9:30 p.m. ETLocation: United Center -- ChicagoTV: ESPN | Live stream: fubo (Try for free)Kentucky vs. Kansas predictionKansas' full team had only been practicing together for only three (!) weeks. Then starting guard Melvin Council Jr. broke his foot Monday, forcing Bill Self to recalibrate again. Kansas has the more talented roster on paper, but I wouldn't be surprised if there are still some kinks to be ironed out that were not exposed in romps over solid mid-majors like Fordham and Middle Tennessee. Is Kentucky good enough to press those hot spots? Maybe. Kentucky's 3-point shooting is the path to popping the upset. Kansas does not profile as a high-volume 3-point shooting team with Trey Kaufman-Renn, Tre White, Tyran Stokes and Keanu Dawes on the floor together. On the other hand, Milan Momcilovic is the best shooter in the sport. If Kentucky can rebound and run, it is very capable of drilling double-digit treys. That's rarely going to be in the range of potential outcomes for Kansas, who will rely heavily on paint points and free throws to score efficiently.
The Council injury likely means Self will go big, sacrificing some of the pace for even more rebounding. A front line of Dawes, Stokes and Kaufman-Renn might not make many 3s, but it creates some awkward matchups for Kentucky. Can Momcilovic defend Stokes without fouling a freshman who is a foul-drawing machine? Does Kentucky ditch that idea altogether and put a bulldog veteran guard like Zoom Diallo onto Stokes, stay home on everyone else and try to bait Stokes into taking a million shots over a smaller defender? Making Stokes one-dimensional is better than allowing him to shred as a scorer and creator. Kansas' offensive rebounding feels inevitable, but Kentucky's shooting and length make it very live. Its up-and-down guards just need to play clean in this one, or UK is dead on arrival. The pick: Kentucky +5.5

title: Why NFL trade deadline evolved from afterthought to hectic: In-season transaction boom is league's new normal - CBS Sports
description: After a record-breaking trade deadline in 2025 and with an active transaction wire in 2026, the times are a-chang
body:
After a record-breaking trade deadline in 2025 and with an active transaction wire in 2026, the times are a-changin' in the NFL
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:31 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Less than a decade ago, it was common for the NFL to feature single-digit trades during the course of the regular season. The trade deadline was generally a snoozer in comparison to that of the other major American professional sports leagues, and the number of moves made at the buzzer could often be counted on one hand. That could not be further from the case anymore.Twenty-four hours out from the 2026 trade deadline, there were 10 in-season trades in the books. That number will balloon in the final hours before the clock strikes 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 10. Star players could be on the move as Super Bowl contenders gear up for the stretch run and teams falling out of contention seek to jumpstart their rebuilds with premium draft capital. Basketball and baseball fans are used to seeing this flurry of transactions, but it is still relatively new to football fans. Just like in the other leagues, though, this boom is becoming the NFL's new normal.Last year, there were 22 trades from the first day of the regular season through the deadline. That was the most in any year since at least 1995, according to NFL Research. A whopping 12 players and 14 picks were exchanged on deadline day alone. General managers were busier than ever. That was the extreme continuation of a trend that has been in effect since the mid-2010s, in which front offices mortgage their futures for instant-impact players or, conversely, sell off their most valuable assets to hoard draft picks.Only once from 2010 through 2017 did the NFL log 12 or more in-season trades, according to the Spotrac trade tracker. Something flipped towards the end of the decade, because that number now represents the low-water mark since 2018.

                                                                    CBS Sports
                                                            Why the sudden uptick? There are fundamental processes in the NFL that make this league more trade-averse than other sports leagues, but changes to the calendar and new front-office philosophies have created pathways for teams to bypass some of the roadblocks.Here are the factors at play.Why in-season trades used to be uncommonTrading players in the NFL is not as simple as matching salaries. That is largely why player-for-player trades remain so rare. The way contracts are structured, with teams spreading bonuses out across multiple years, taking on dead money and being on the hook for some of the salary owed to the players they trade away, is sometimes prohibitive. Plus, the NFL has a hard salary cap, so unlike in the NBA, where teams use exceptions to go over the cap, or in MLB, where wealthy owners can pony up as much money as they please, all deals have to result in both teams remaining under that firm number.Football is also not as plug-and-play as other sports. There are massive playbooks to learn, especially at the offensive skill positions. There is incredibly important timing to perfect, particularly for the quarterback-wide receiver tandem. With 11 players on the field at all times and complicated schemes to comprehend, anyone who joins a lineup in the middle of the season has a lot of learning to do on the fly.
The brevity of a 17-game regular season also keeps a larger percentage of the league in playoff contention deeper into the year compared to 82- or 162-game campaigns. The lack of non-contenders means fewer teams are willing to sell, and thus there is a smaller volume of available players.Draft picks are also immensely valuable since teams have so many roster spots to fill. And at the same time, rosters are so large that fringe players around the 53-man cutoff can simply be released if the potential trade package is undesirable.Calendar changes shift contention windowsUntil 2011, the NFL trade deadline was extremely early in the season. It landed on the Tuesday following Week 6, which was well before the midway point of the campaign. Teams were often still attempting to figure out where they stood in the pecking order when it came time to lock in their rosters. How could a general manager shop one of his stars on an expiring contract when they were not sure whether their team was in the mix for a postseason berth or not? They rarely did.
That changed in 2012 when the NFL and NFL Players Association agreed to move the deadline back by two weeks to the Tuesday following Week 8. And not long after the league adopted a 17th regular-season game, it moved the deadline back another week to where it stands now: The Tuesday after Week 9, which is effectively the midseason point.It is far clearer where teams stand in the playoff picture after Week 9 than after Week 6. Look no further than the Indianapolis Colts, who emerged as one of the NFL's most aggressive sellers this year. Through six games, they were 2-4 and competitive enough in a couple of their losses to believe that they could right the ship. Now, after nine games, they are a measly 2-7 and own a five-game losing streak. Clearly out of the postseason hunt, they moved on from perennial Pro Bowlers in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner."F them picks"Perhaps the single most impactful change in the rise of in-season trades comes from the mentality surrounding draft picks. While the value of Day 1 picks in the NFL is still tremendous, it is more common now than ever to see general managers move that sacred capital for players who can help them win at the highest level right away instead of a couple of years down the line. Nowhere is this clearer than in Los Angeles, where Rams general manager Les Snead birthed the "F them picks" mantra.
Les Snead's top blockbuster trades2016: Traded six picks to move up to No. 1 overall2018: Traded first-round pick for Brandin Cooks2019: Traded three picks for Jalen Ramsey2021: Traded Jared Goff, three picks for Matthew Stafford2026: Traded Jared Verse, three picks for Myles Garrett AND traded four picks for Trent McDuffieEach of those moves opened or extended the Rams' championship contention windows. They are bets on current stars and their ability to keep playing at a high level, compared to the risk of boom-or-bust picks in the late first round. In order to balance the roster, Snead relies on finding diamonds in the rough in the later rounds, which he has been highly successful at pulling off.This model delivered a Super Bowl and proved to other teams that it is a viable strategy for roster construction. In the copycat league that is the NFL, the Rams are no longer the only team to go all in to fuel championship runs.Snead even has direct disciples putting his methodology to practice in other places. Jacksonville Jaguars general manager James Gladstone worked under Snead's tutelage in various roles for nine years before he landed a GM job of his own. On Monday, he pulled off two trades in which he swapped draft picks for immediate-impact players. They may not have been Day 1 picks, but they were draft capital nonetheless.
General managers get craftyDraft picks are still gold, even in this era where they are moved like never before. General managers who want the best of both worlds -- to hoard picks and secure immediate impacts -- can balance the two, but they have to be creative. Enter the pick swap. Instead of one team netting a draft pick while the other loses one, pick swaps allow teams to generate value in the aggregate while retaining at least some capital. If a player is valued around a late-Day 2 pick, the buying team could send a second-rounder and receive a Day 3 pick in return along with that player.Compensatory picks also give general managers the flexibility to take swings at available players. If there is a veteran on an expiring contract who can join a team as a half-season rental, the buying franchise may give up a third-round pick or worse to acquire them, knowing that they can recoup the pick if the player leaves in free agency.Gladstone himself pulled off a masterful move ahead of Tuesday's deadline by factoring compensatory picks into the equation. He reached a deal with the New Orleans Saints that sent Davon Godchaux to Jacksonville in exchange for a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick. That pick would become a 2027 sixth-rounder if the Jaguars acquire one through another trade or through the compensatory formula. In essence, Gladstone traded a pick he does not even own yet.
Is this the new normal?So many things in football are cyclical, but the surge in trade deadline action has staying power. Changes at the league level with regard to scheduling have made it more viable, and general managers are as aggressive as ever in a "what have you done for me lately" world. Now that front offices have another tool at their disposal in roster construction, it will only become more mainstream. The cat is out of the bag, and it will be hard to put it back in.

title: Winners and losers from the first week of women's hoops: JuJu Watkins returns, two players get turned around - CBS Sports
description: College basketball is back, and we're recapping the good, the bad and the weird of the first week
body:
College basketball is back, and we're recapping the good, the bad and the weird of the first week
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:58 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The 2026-27 women's college basketball season is already off to a rousing start, and spoiler alert: South Carolina is still very good! The Gamecocks got off to a 2-0 start, with both wins coming over ranked teams, and Dawn Staley's squad firmly looks like the team to beat this season.
        
            
                Women's college basketball rankings: Michigan up to No. 2 in AP Top 25 after UConn upset
                
                    Lindsay Gibbs                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
But below them in the rankings, there were storylines galore. It was a week filled with records, including the debut of the tallest player in women's college basketball history, Texas Tech's 7-foot-1 Stephanie Okechukwu, and the most lopsided game in women's Division I history, LSU's 109-point blowout of Texas Southern. It also included a vanishing event, a historic upset, an iconic return, a couple of headline-generating gaffes and even a dazzling debut from a WNBA draftee.Without further ado, here are winners and losers from the opening week of action:Winner: The Michigan WolverinesThere's no reason to get cute off the top. On Thursday night at the Crisler Center, the Wolverines got one of the biggest wins in program history, defeating then-No. 2 UConn, 77-66. Coming into the game, the Huskies had won 39 regular-season games in a row, dating back to Feb. 6, 2025.
The win took Michigan from No. 5 to No. 2 in the AP poll, and sent a message that the Wolverines are a true Final Four contender. It was a marquee moment for head coach Kim Barnes Arico and her star-studded junior class, most of whom came into the program together as freshmen to do something special."That's why we came here. We had belief in coach. We had belief in the program, and we wanted to help build it, to take it places it hasn't been," guard Olivia Olson said. "I'm just proud to be part of it."Te'Yala Delfosse, one of the more unheralded members of that class, led the way with 22 points, nine rebounds and four 3-pointers. Olson added 10 points and eight rebounds, while Syla Swords had 10 points and five boards.
Loser: Sense of directionThere are always some kinks to work out early in the season, but last week that notion was taken to new heights not once, but twice. Two players in two separate games in Division I women's basketball on Friday shot the ball into the wrong basket. Yes, we had two basketball own goals. 
The first came from Karma Wynn of Northwestern State, who got mixed up during a full-court press after her team inbounded the ball in the first quarter and scored two points for Arkansas. Arkansas ended up winning the game 89-59, so Wynn's basket didn't decide the game by any means.However, later that day, an own goal almost did impact the final result when Emma Christiano of New Mexico State also got turned around after intercepting an inbound play. That came at a crucial time in the game, though, with Southern Utah up 61-60 with 20.9 seconds remaining. Christiano thought she had put her team ahead, but instead she extended Southern Utah's lead to 63-60.
Christiano's teammates had her back, though; New Mexico State scored four points in the final 20 seconds to win the game 64-63. We all do inexplicable things sometimes, and hopefully both Wynn and Christiano can laugh at their mistakes. And hey, at the very least, since they shared the gaffe, they can take the heat off of one another.Winner: JuJu Watkins' returnAfter 588 days on the sidelines, JuJu Watkins officially returned to the women's college basketball world last week and immediately showed the world what it has been missing.In her first game, which No. 3 USC won 100-68 over UNLV, Watkins had 21 points, five rebounds, two steals and a block in 25 minutes. The only blip on that day was her shooting, as she was 0 of 5 from outside. However, she immediately got back on track in the second game, with a staggering 32 points, 16 rebounds, six assists, five steals and one block in a 118-40 victory over Utah State. In that game, Watkins was 10 of 19 from the field for 52.6% and 4 of 7 from 3-point land for 57.1%.
It will be interesting to see how Watkins holds up against tougher competition, and we won't have to wait long; on Sunday, Nov. 15 USC travels to Greenville to face No. 1 South Carolina. Go ahead and clear your schedules.
        
            
                JuJu Watkins returns after 588 days: USC star on family, the ACL tear and why 'there is no if' for the Trojans
                
                    Erica Ayala                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Loser: The Foundry ClassicBecause of Michigan's big win over UConn, Duke fell from No. 4 to No. 5 in the rankings this week despite getting off to a 2-0 start with fairly comfortable wins over Green Bay and Florida Atlantic. However, the box scores don't accurately describe how bizarre the first week of the regular season was for Kara Lawson and her team.Originally -- and up until last Thursday -- Duke was scheduled to play their second game of the season against North Texas at the Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. The game was to be a homecoming for Duke junior Arianna Robinson and freshman Bella Flemings, who grew up in the area. The game was part of The Foundry Classic, which was billed as a two-day event that would see players from each team "participate through dedicated residency spaces for each program, providing opportunities for students to engage with college athletes beyond the basketball court."
Among other things, Lawson and North Texas head coach Jason Burton were supposed to be part of a panel on Saturday evening, the night before the game.But on Thursday evening, USA Today reported that Duke was reaching out to teams in other conferences in "urgent need of a replacement game" for the weekend. And on Friday, both Duke and North Texas announced that the game had been canceled "due to circumstances beyond the control of participating institutions." It is currently unknown what exactly transpired, but it seems The Foundry Classic never materialized.Duke was able to schedule a last-minute road game at Florida Atlantic on Sunday, which it won, 78-56. 
Winner: Addi Mack's second half against South CarolinaAs exciting as the first week of the season was, there aren't many individual performances that I'm still going to be thinking about come March. The exception to that rule might be Addi Mack's second half against South Carolina in the season opener in Paris.Maryland was down 28 points at the half and 31 points in the third quarter, but with 46 seconds left in the game, the Gamecocks were holding onto a six-point lead by their claws. South Carolina ended up holding onto a 101-93 victory, but the Terrapins were so impressive in a loss that they went up one place in the rankings to No. 19.And it was Mack who powered the valiant comeback attempt, with 31 points in the second half, even bettering Gabby Williams' second-half performance in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals -- by points, at least. For the game, Mack was 14 of 20 from the field and 6 of 10 from outside for 35 points, six assists, three rebounds and two steals. Even though the performance came in a loss, it deserves to be a winner.
Loser: The 2026 Chicago SkyYes, I know that this is a women's college basketball piece, and that the Chicago Sky got dunked on plenty during the WNBA season after the team traded Angel Reese and saw her immediately take the Atlanta Dream to the Finals. But they're in the spotlight again because of the performance of Ajša Sivka, a Slovenian player whom the Sky actually drafted No. 10 overall in the 2025 WNBA draft.Sivka didn't join the team in 2025, and this spring she opted to sign with the Kentucky Wildcats in lieu of joining the Sky for the 2026 season. And she is acclimating just fine to the college game -- on Sunday against N.C. State, Sivka had 32 points, five rebounds and three assists in Kentucky's 93-78 win. Her efficiency was more impressive than her stat line -- she was 11 of 17 from the field and a staggering 8 of 12 from outside.In press, she said that she chose to come to Kentucky because of the development she could get under head coach Kenny Brooks, noting that the individual work this summer has already helped her improve. 
"I just wanted to be ready and feel confident once I go there," she said, referring to the WNBA. Brooks said she is "definitely one of the best players in the country."The Sky do retain her WNBA rights, so they might be winners in the long run. But they certainly could have used a shooter like her in the 2026 season.

title: Gotham FC move NWSL semi to Icahn Stadium over pitch quality concerns - CBS Sports
description: Gotham were originally set to play Sunday's semifinal at Sports Illustrated Stadium, where the pitch was describe
body:
Gotham were originally set to play Sunday's semifinal at Sports Illustrated Stadium, where the pitch was described as 'atrocious' following their quarterfinal match against the Seattle Reign
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:46 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Gotham FC will play Sunday's NWSL semifinal against the Kansas City Current at Icahn Stadium over concerns about the quality of the pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium, which was described as "atrocious" during the team's quarterfinal win over the Seattle Reign.The NWSL Shield winners announced the venue shift on Monday, less than a week before the semifinal. Icahn Stadium is a smaller venue on Manhattan's Randall's Island that seats 5,000 and has been sparingly used by Gotham, who have played the vast majority of their home games at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, N.J. since 2021. Sports Illustrated Stadium seats 25,000 and welcomed nearly 13,000 for Sunday's 1-0 win over the Reign.The quarterfinal match, though, was marred by complaints about the playing surface from both teams. Reign head coach Laura Harvey described the field as "shit" in a post-match interview with ESPN, while captain Jess Fishlock called it "atrocious." Gotham head coach Juan Carlos Amoros also apologized for the quality of the surface after the NWSL fined the club $10,000 in the build-up to the quarterfinal match."We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth," captain Tierna Davidson said in a statement on Monday. "What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league, or our fans deserve. The quality of the game is not up for debate, so we've made the difficult decision to move to Icahn Stadium on Sunday. A smaller stadium means many of you will not be there, and that is the hardest part of this decision. You have turned every ground where we have played into home, and that does not change on Sunday. We have never needed a perfect setting to make a place ours. Bring everything you have on Sunday, and we will leave it all on the field."
The pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium appeared to show the wear and tear from recent events, not least of which was Gotham's regular season slate. Gotham are the secondary tenants at the venue, which is owned by New Jersey's Hudson County but counts MLS' Red Bull New York as the primary tenants and operators of the facility. The stadium was also the site of a rugby doubleheader the weekend before Gotham's quarterfinal against the Reign, which led Gotham midfielder Jaelin Howell to describe the surface as "sandy" and "unstable."The Red Bulls will still play a friendly on Saturday at Sports Illustrated Stadium against Club America. The friendly will take place during the men's international break, so several first-team players will miss the match, which will serve as the final game of their season since they missed out on the MLS Cup playoffs for a second season in a row."We wish Gotham FC the best of luck in their semifinal at Icahn Stadium," Red Bull New York told CBS Sports in a statement. "We look forward to our match on Saturday at Sports Illustrated Stadium."
Not Gotham's first trip to IcahnGotham have staged two games at Icahn Stadium in the last year and change – a Concacaf W Champions Cup group stage match in 2025 and their 3-2 win over the Reign in July. There is the perception of convenience for the club's fans based in the city of New York, who would otherwise have to trek to New Jersey to attend a game. As far as public transportation goes, though, Icahn Stadium is only accessible via the M35 bus; a footbridge connecting Randall's Island to 125th Street is also an option, as is driving to the stadium."It's nice for folks who live in New York to have a somewhat closer venue," Jen Muller, a longtime member of the official Gotham supporters group Cloud 9, told CBS Sports last year. "I know it's not ideal for a lot of them, too, because there's one bus that comes here, but you adapt."The pitch at Icahn Stadium, which has also hosted New York City FC II matches this year, is not expected to be an issue and was not during the Concacaf match in 2025.
"I don't really want to talk too much about it, but the Sports Illustrated Stadium has traditionally been the best pitch in the league," Amoros said at the time, "and the last couple of games, it's definitely been far away from that, so this pitch here is outstanding."Logistics plague NWSL playoffsGotham's move to Icahn comes despite the fact that they avoided a scheduling conflict with Sunday's results. The NWSL's broadcast slots for this year's semifinals were Saturday at 12 p.m. ET on CBS and Paramount+ and Sunday at 3 p.m. ET on ABC; the Washington Spirit will host the Utah Royals on Saturday, while Gotham will take on the Current on Sunday.For Gotham, the Sunday time slot was the preferred option because of a pre-existing scheduling conflict with the Red Bulls' Saturday friendly against Club America. They had to wait out the result of the Spirit's quarterfinal with the Portland Thorns, though, since the Thorns would have been unable to host a semifinal at 9 a.m. local time. Gotham seemed destined to return to Sports Illustrated Stadium once they avoided the scheduling conflict but the quality of the pitch caused new concerns.
The Spirit, meanwhile, avoided a scheduling conflict of their own. They were originally set to host the Royals at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., home of the NFL's Washington Commanders, because their usual venue of Audi Field was instead hosting Secretaries' Cup, a Division III college football game between the United States Merchant Marine Academy and the United States Coast Guard Academy. The college football game has since been pushed to a later slot that day, Spirit CEO Kim Stone crediting Audi Field owners D.C. United and sponsor Lafayette Federal Credit Union for underwriting "the additional costs necessary to bring this semifinal match home."The issues stem from the fact that many NWSL teams are secondary tenants in their home stadiums, the Spirit included – MLS' D.C. United own and operate Audi Field. Some, like the Royals and the Orlando Pride, benefit from sharing ownership groups with MLS clubs, while the Current own and operate CPKC Stadium. The rest often rent the local MLS team's stadium, Gotham and the Spirit included, but it creates other unique conflicts for teams with more control over their venues. The Current's quarterfinal against Angel City on Saturday, for example, kicked off at 11 a.m. local time in order to fit the broadcast slot on CBS.

title: Fantasy football Week 10 risers and fallers: Bryce Young surges, Stafford slips - CBS Sports
description: Bryce Young is climbing the Fantasy ranks after a breakout performance, while Matthew Stafford's struggles raise
body:
Bryce Young is climbing the Fantasy ranks after a breakout performance, while Matthew Stafford's struggles raise concerns
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:48 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Prominent players we projected last week that we are not projecting to play in Week 10 as of Monday evening: Josh Jacobs, Rhamondre Stevenson, Omar Cooper Jr., Xavier Worthy, Ladd McConkey, Jake FergusonAt the bottom of this article are my Week 10 projections for quarterback, running back, wide receiver, and tight end. They will be updated throughout the week as we get more information. Risers Bryce Young, QB, Panthers
In some ways, Young was always going to be a Week 10 riser. That's because he faced the Broncos in Week 9 and will play against the Saints in Week 10. What we didn't expect was Young throwing for 276 yards and three touchdowns against one of the best pass defenses in the NFL. Young has now produced multiple touchdowns in five of eight starts and at least 276 yards passing in six of eight. Against the Saints, he looks close to a must-start option.
C.J. Stroud, QB, Texans
Stroud gets the Browns this week, which is not a good matchup for QBs at all. I'm not sure it matters. With Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Kayshon Boutte, Xavier Hutchinson, and Marvin Harrison, Stroud has arguably the deepest collection of pass catchers in the NFL. The Texans' inability to sustain a run game has led to Stroud throwing 35 times per game, and he's averaging a very impressive eight yards per attempt. I am not sure I see a matchup left in the Fantasy regular season that will cause me to rank Stroud outside of the top 12.Breece Hall, RB, Jets
In his first game back, Hall had 18 touches. That's enough to move him back inside my top 20 running backs, especially with four teams on a bye and more injuries to the position in Week 9. I actually think against the Bills you may be able to start both Hall and Braelon Allen as RB2s. They face the Bills in Week 10 and heading into Monday night, the Bills have given up the second-most points to opposing running backs.Derrick Henry and Zay Flowers, Ravens
I am not sure Jacoby Brissett can save the Ravens season, but I do expect him to save the Fantasy season for Henry and Flowers. Brissett has been mostly bad so far this season, but still levels above Joe Fagnano. Teams will have to respect the pass at least a little bit, which should open up running lanes for Henry. Flowers has already proven that he can deliver with Tyler Huntley, and projects as a borderline top 12 wide receiver once again. What will be interesting is the Ravens run/pass split. Brissett has led a pass-heavy offense in Arizona the past two years. I would expect a balanced approach from Baltimore, especially against the Chargers.
Jordyn Tyson, WR, Saints
I'm not ready to rank Tyson as a starter yet, but I can see the light at the end of the tunnel. He was second on the team in targets in his debut despite running just 34.8% of the team's routes. I expect him to be over 50% this week and inch towards 75% in the coming month. This week he may not need more than 50% in a shootout against the Panthers. View Tyson as a low-end WR3, but he has more reason for optimism than most of the guys projected in that range.FallersMatthew Stafford, QB, Rams
If Puka Nacua's knee injury is serious, Stafford may fall out of the top 24, but even with Nacua, Stafford is a faller. He already has his most interceptions in a season since 2023 and he hasn't reached even 230 yards since Week 5. His 6.9 yards per pass attempt this year is tied for his worst mark since joining the Rams. Stafford could still turn this around, but we need to see it before we want to start him again. Hopefully Terrance Ferguson will help whenever he gets back.Quinshon Judkins, RB, Browns
If we can't trust Judkins against the Saints, I don't know who we can trust him against. He even got an extra 10 minutes in Week 9 thanks to overtime and still only scored 5.5 PPR Fantasy points. The two major problems are horrible rush efficiency and Dylan Sampson hogging the running back targets. We have no reason to expect either to change in Week 10 when the Browns take on the Texans.
Devin Singletary, RB, Giants
This is actually good news: Cam Skattebo is expected back! Singletary should go back to a role on third downs and the two-minute drill, which makes him a desperation flex at best. Skattebo is ranked about where Singletary was last week, around RB24. This is a huge opportunity for the second-year back even if the Commanders run defense has been good for most of the season.Nico Collins, WR, Texans
It is rare that we have a quarterback as a riser and his number one receiver as a faller. The problem is that Collins, despite an amazing touchdown catch on Sunday, barely looks like a WR1. Collins hasn't seen more than five targets in a game since Week 5. In his last three games, he has a 14.4% snap share and he's only played 62.9% of the offensive snaps. The Texans have a heavy rotation at receiver right now and it is capping Collins' upside. You're still probably starting him as a WR2 but he is no longer a must-start in leagues where you only start two receivers.Brenton Strange, TE, Jaguars
This has less to do with Strange than it does the Jaguars blowing everyone out. Trevor Lawrence has thrown a combined 40 passes in his last two games. Strange's best games came when the volume was much higher. This week they are 10-point favorites against the Titans. There is no reason to hope for more than 25 pass attempts from Lawrence. Strange is still a high-end TE2 but he will probably need a touchdown to score double-digit Fantasy points.

title: Kansas guard Melvin Council Jr. out until Big 12 play starts after breaking foot in practice - CBS Sports
description: Council started both of Kanas' first two games and is now expected to be out until a least January
body:
Council started both of Kanas' first two games and is now expected to be out until a least January

        Kansas will be without starting guard Melvin Council Jr. until at least January after he suffered a broken foot during practice, the program announced on Monday. The Jayhawks are set to face No. 24 Kentucky on Tuesday in Chicago in the second leg of the Champions Classic."Melvin broke the fifth metatarsal in his foot during Monday's practice and will have surgery in the next couple of days," Kansas coach Bill Self said. "We expect a full recovery and we're hopeful he will return around the start of the conference season."Council, who is playing this season on an injunction after being granted a fifth year of eligibility, started in each of Kansas' first two games of the season against Middle Tennessee and Fordham. He finished with 10 points, seven assists, six rebounds and two steals during the 30-point win against Fordham on opening night last week.
        
            
                Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase
                
                    Adam Finkelstein                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The former Wagner and St. Bonaventure guard transferred to Kansas ahead of the 2025-26 season and started 35 games for the Jayhawks, averaging 12.7 points, 5.1 assists and 5.0 rebounds. Council and Tre White — two starters from last season's team — were granted a fifth year of eligibility weeks before the program's season opener.
In addition to adding White and Council back to the roster, Kansas also added former Purdue star forward Trey Kaufman-Renn. Kaufman-Renn spent the first five seasons of his college career with the Boilermakers before enrolling at Kansas ahead of the start of the season, where he is playing on an injunction.Who steps up now for Kansas?Losing Council is a big loss for Kansas. He was a microwave scorer for the Jayhawks last season. He brought extra energy while playing with both the first and second units. When star guard Darryn Peterson missed extensive time last season due to cramping issues, Council stepped up on the offensive end of the floor.Now, others will have to do the same in his absenceIn Kansas' season-opener, Self didn't start Kaufman-Renn and went with a lineup of Taylen Kinney/White/Council/Tyran Stokes and Christian Reeves. Reeves came off the bench during Kansas' second game of the season when Kaufman-Renn was elevated to the starting lineup.

        
            
                UCLA, Virginia jump in AP Top 25 poll after big wins; Arizona, Arkansas drop in college basketball rankings
                
                    Cameron Salerno                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
With Council out, Self will have options on how he wants to replace his production in the starting lineup. Two options are Keanu Dawes or Leroy Blyden Jr., who played the most minutes off the bench during the Jayhawks' last game. None of Kansas' starters played more than 22 minutes in the second game of the season because it was a blowout, so expect the starters to play significantly more against Kentucky on Tuesday.Stokes, who is the projected No. 1 pick in the 2027 NBA Draft, scored eight points in 21 minutes against Middle Tennessee. His minutes and production are both expected to increase as Kansas' schedule gets tougher with games against Kentucky, UNLV, Villanova, UConn and Ohio State on the schedule.Kansas' opening game of Big 12 play is against West Virginia on Jan. 2. The lone ranked conference opponent the Jayhawks face during the first month of the season is No. 23 BYU on Jan. 9. The first real test in conference play will come on the road against No. 8 Houston on Feb. 1.

body:
Sending Jonathan Taylor to Green Bay and reuniting Kirk Cousins with Minnesota headline moves that could spark playoff pushes
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026

        The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, and here are four trades I'd like to see happen that could impact Fantasy Football rosters. Let's hope a change of scenery could open up production for players who can help us for the rest of the season and into the Fantasy playoffs.As of Monday afternoon, we've had two offensive skill players dealt with Jacoby Brissett (Arizona to Baltimore) and Marvin Harrison Jr. (Arizona to Houston). A handful of defensive players have already been dealt, including Jeffery Simmons (Tennessee to Chicago), DeForest Buckner (Indianapolis to San Francisco), Joey Porter Jr. (Pittsburgh to Dallas) and Jessie Bates III (Atlanta to Jacksonville).What will happen prior to Tuesday's deadline? I can't wait to see, and it could make for a fun week on the waiver wire as well. For now, let's make some fake trades.1. RB Jonathan Taylor to the PackersThe Colts aren't going to give Taylor away, and the Packers need running back help with Josh Jacobs (finger) now expected to miss three weeks. It could get messy once Jacobs is healthy, but acquiring Taylor would signal that Green Bay plans to use him as a workhorse. The Packers' offensive line hasn't been ideal, but Taylor's presence could certainly improve things in Green Bay. It would also be a fun story to see Taylor play for the Packers since he played collegiately at Wisconsin. Taylor would remain a No. 1 Fantasy running back in Green Bay, and this trade would allow the Colts to use Seth McGowan as a starter, giving him value as a low-end No. 2 running back or flex in all formats.
2. QB Kirk Cousins to the VikingsCousins has been great with the Raiders, scoring at least 22.5 Fantasy points in six of nine games, and I'd love to see him reunited with the Vikings. He had an excellent run in Minnesota from 2018-23, averaging at least 20.6 Fantasy points in five of six seasons, and he would do great being back with Kevin O'Connell. This trade would rejuvenate Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson, and Cousins would remain a low-end No. 1 Fantasy quarterback. It would also allow the Raiders to start Fernando Mendoza, and we're all excited to see Mendoza play. 3. WR Josh Downs to the 49ersThe 49ers might be desperate enough for receiver help that they trade for Downs and Keenan Allen from the Colts. Mike Evans (Achilles), Deebo Samuel (hamstring), Christian Kirk (knee), and De'Zhaun Stribling (ankle) are all injured, and San Francisco could use a playmaker like Downs. He scored at least 12.7 PPR points in two of his first three games and has been a disaster since, with one game over 8.7 PPR points in his past six outings. But with the 49ers, Downs could emerge as a No. 2 Fantasy receiver in all leagues, especially if Evans and Samuel remain out.
4. WR Brian Thomas Jr. to the ChiefsThomas needs to leave Jacksonville, and any opportunity would be a good chance for him to resurrect his career in Fantasy and reality. He's averaging just 4.2 PPR points per game in 2026, which is a far cry from his rookie campaign when he was a star at 16.7 PPR points per game. The Chiefs won't feature Thomas, but I'm not sure any team will at this point. That said, with Tyquan Thornton (ankle) on IR and now Xavier Worthy (hamstring), the Chiefs need playmakers in the passing game. Patrick Mahomes would benefit greatly with Thomas as a downfield threat, and he could regain value as a starter in three-receiver leagues by going to Kansas City.

title: College football's 10 worst coordinator hires of last five years - CBS Sports
description: From historic buyouts to collapsed offenses, high-profile missteps at Michigan, Oregon, USC and Oklahoma prove th
body:
From historic buyouts to collapsed offenses, high-profile missteps at Michigan, Oregon, USC and Oklahoma prove that missing on a play-caller can quickly derail a national contender
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:34 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The job of a college football head coach has never been less focused on coaching football. In that sense, assistant coaches and coordinator hires have never been more important. On Sunday, Michigan fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck, who came to Ann Arbor with coach Kyle Whittingham from Utah. Last season, he coordinated a top-10 offense. This year, he is owed more than $10 million for less than one year of work, believed to be the largest buyout ever for an assistant coach. However, Michigan is not alone. Oregon also fired offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer in his first season. Oklahoma canned Ben Arbuckle midway through his second season. The level of patience is going down. With the pressures facing coaching staffs in 2026, bad hires cost a program more than ever. Here are 10 of the worst coordinator hires of the past five years, including a few that tanked College Football Playoff teams just this season. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Dino Babers, OC | Arizona | 2024Babers was hailed as a strong hire for first-year coach Brent Brennan. He was coming off 10 years as a head coach, including several solid offenses at Syracuse. Babers was hired to maintain after a historic 10-win season. Instead, his offense completely collapsed. Arizona went 4-8 in Babers' lone season as offensive coordinator, sandwiched between a 10-win and nine-win season. Quarterback Noah Fifita dropped from 72% to 60% completion, 8.6 to 6.9 yards per attempt and doubled his highest interception mark. Really, the greatest indictment of Babers' tenure? Watching Fifita's production in every other season of his career. 

        
            
                Loyal to a fault: These 5 teams are paying the price for sticking with familiar faces in 2026
                
                    John Talty                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Todd Grantham, DC | Oklahoma State | 2025Before the 2025 season, Oklahoma State coach Mike Gundy told CBS Sports that he essentially couldn't get his top assistant choices. That sure looked to be the case during an unbelievably embarrassing 1-11 campaign, in which Grantham was fired after only four games despite a fully guaranteed three-year contract. In two games against Power Four teams, Grantham's unit gave up a combined 114 points against No. 6 Oregon and Baylor. The 69-3 loss against Oregon was one of the worst performances in Oklahoma State history, if not the worst. Firing Grantham was one of interim coach Doug Meacham's very first moves. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Alex Grinch, DC | USC | 2022Grinch actually wasn't a terrible hire at Oklahoma in 2019, taking the defense from terrible to solid after transitioning from Mike Stoops. However, Riley should have noticed the regression and made a change when he took the heralded job at USC. 
Instead, Grinch led some of the most stunningly terrible defenses in America with the Trojans. USC ranked No. 119 in total defense, allowing 432.8 yards per game. They allowed 6.3 yards per play against Power Four competition before Riley finally pulled the plug. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Freddie Kitchens, OC | North Carolina | 2025Kitchens seemed like a no-brainer for Bill Belichick at North Carolina. The former Cleveland Browns head coach called plays at the NFL level and spent multiple years as run game coordinator with the Tar Heels before Belichick took over. Instead, Kitchens led a wildly unorganized unit. The Tar Heels started their season by being held to a combined 23 points against UCF and TCU, and it barely got any better. UNC went 2-1 in games where they scored at least 20 points. They just… only scored 20 points against three Power Four opponents.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Seth Littrell, OC | Oklahoma | 2024It's hard to fully evaluate Littrell, who was a sensational offensive mind at North Carolina and North Texas. The Sooners dealt with major injuries, had a lemon in quarterback Jackson Arnold, and were a disaster on the offensive line -- an issue that persists under the current regime. But for his seven games in the job, Oklahoma was absolutely horrendous, recording their worst offense through seven games since 1961. A Red River embarrassment was the final straw, losing 34-3 against Texas with a backup quarterback. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Drew Mehringer, OC | Oregon | 2026Oregon coach Dan Lanning has pressed essentially every right button as a head coach, but elevating Mehringer was a disaster. The former co-offensive coordinator and tight ends coach was asked to replace Will Stein, and instead tanked one of the most talented offenses in America. 
The Ducks returned almost everyone, and subsequently fell from No. 5 to 49 in FEI offense. They managed to turn 426 yards of offense into 10 points against Illinois in a stunning 21-10 defeat. Even in the games since Mehringer was fired, the improvements are obvious. Oregon has scored 75 points over the past two games against ranked opponents, including a 41-28 win over No. 12 Ohio State. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Chad Morris, OC | Clemson | 2026Like so many times before, Clemson coach Dabo Swinney tried to get the band back together in 2026. That included hiring offensive coordinator Chad Morris, who had not called plays at the college level since 2020 at Auburn. 
Naturally, it's led to one of the most disorganized offenses in America. The Tigers rank No. 115 in total offense and No. 127 in yards per play, the fourth-worst Power Four unit in the country. The performance marks a full-yard-per-play regression compared to last year's disappointing unit and puts Swinney on the hottest of seats.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Mike Shula, OC, South Carolina | 2025The former Alabama head coach and NFL offensive coordinator was brought to South Carolina in hopes of helping quarterback LaNorris Sellers take the next step. Instead, Shula absolutely tanked Sellers' stock and nearly got coach Shane Beamer fired. Sellers, previously regarded as a first-round pick, regressed in every category as Shula tried to turn him into a pocket passer. His efficiency suffered the most, falling from 66% completion to 61%. South Carolina is well on its way to two eight-win seasons in three years -- with a 4-8 under Shula sandwiched in between. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Tony White, DC, Florida State | 2025What sets White apart on this list is the sheer magnitude of the move at the time. White was a major up-and-comer as a defensive coordinator at Syracuse and Nebraska, leading the Huskers to a top-20 defense in 2024. He signed a contract that averaged $1.6 million over three years. There were some early returns at Florida State, but they were incredibly short-lived. Florida State fell to No. 122 in total defense in White's second season, as coach Mike Norvell was ultimately fired. In the last three games of Norvell's tenure, they gave up a combined 113 points. When Rick Stockstill was named interim coach, he quickly fired White. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Holman Wiggins, OC | Texas A&M | 2026Wiggins has been one of the most respected wide receiver coaches in the country, and enticed stars KC Concepcion and Mario Craver to College Station just last year. But one year into his tenure as playcaller, it's clear that Wiggins is not ready to lead an offense. 
The Aggies fell from No. 21 to No. 119 in yards per play despite returning many key contributors, including quarterback Marcel Reed. Reed has been the biggest loser by far of the coordinator switch, regressing from a productive dual-threat into a total liability. Reed is sitting at eight touchdowns to eight interceptions, and Texas A&M is likely headed from the College Football Playoff to missing a bowl game. The defense hasn't been great either, but Texas A&M's offense is generationally bad.

        The AFC South-leading Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) are loading up for a run at the Super Bowl just ahead of the trade deadline. After trading for Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates III and New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux, they are trading for another defender Monday afternoon: Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis.The Jaguars are sending the Eagles a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for Davis, the 13th overall pick in the 2022 NFL Draft out of Georgia who was a starter on the Eagles' Super Bowl LIX title team in the 2024 season. Jacksonville doesn't have to worry about a long-term contract with Davis as they do with Bates, since Philadelphia extended Davis on a three-year, $78 million extension this past offseason. 
On Monday alone, the Jaguars have shipped out a 2027 first-round pick, a 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 fifth-round pick, a 2028 sixth-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for the services of Davis, Bates and Godchaux. Jacksonville entered Monday with the No. 2 scoring defense in football (15.1 points per game), and now they are continuing to fortify that side of the ball to help quarterback Trevor Lawrence and the league's No. 4 scoring offense (28.6 points per game) make a push to win the AFC and advance to the Super Bowl. Just a year ago, the New England Patriots made the leap from picking in the top five to winning the conference, and the AFC appears wide open once again, with both the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills each having clear flaws.

title: Rams All-Pro Puka Nacua likely to go on injured reserve with knee, toe injuries - CBS Sports

The Rams will now likely be without both Puka Nacua and Davante Adams

        The Los Angeles Rams (5-4) can't catch a break from the injury. After All-Pro edge rusher Myles Garrett's triumphant return to the lineup in their Week 9 victory over the Washington Commanders, All-Pro wide receiver Puka Nacua is expected to go on injured reserve. Coach Sean McVay told reporters on Monday that Nacua, who is dealing with MCL and PCL sprains in addition to turf toe, will likely go on injured reserve, thus sidelining him for at least four games. That's a massive blow for the Rams as Nacua led the NFL in catches (129), receiving first downs (80) and receiving yards per game (107.2) last season. He is also the NFL's all-time leader in receiving yards per game with a career average of 96.2. This season, he has 70 catches for 715 receiving yards and 4 touchdowns while also adding 41 yards rushing and a touchdown on 7 carries. Nacua leads the Rams in every receiving metric this season while being tied for the team lead in receiving touchdowns with six-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Davante Adams. In 2026, he represents 27.6% of the Rams' team target share, which is the eighth-highest rate in the entire NFL this season. Nacua now joins Adams (hamstring) on injured reserve. Adams went down with a hamstring injury in the team's Week 6 loss against the Arizona Cardinals, and McVay said at the time that Adams would be expected to miss 6 to 10 weeks. That means the earliest Adams could return is against his former team, the Green Bay Packers, in Week 12 on Nov. 25. The earliest Nacua could return is Week 15 against the Dallas Cowboys on Dec. 20, if he misses a minimum of four games. Fortunately for Nacua, Los Angeles' Week 11 bye also gives him an extra week to heal up.After Nacua and Adams, Los Angeles running back Kyren Williams leads the Rams in targets (46), and he is No. 2 on the team in catches with 36. Tight end Tyler Higbee is No. 3 on the team in receiving yards with 287 after both Nacua and Adams, and tight end Davis Allen (two receiving touchdowns) is No. 3 on the team in receiving touchdowns behind Los Angeles' two injured star wideouts. 
Quarterback Matthew Stafford will have to make some magic happen with a depleted arsenal of playmakers, in addition to leaning on Williams and Blake Corum in the run game, in order to maximize the Rams' "all in" 2.0 run in 2026.

title: Cardinals' Gardner Minshew feared to have suffered a torn UCL, could be out for season, per report - CBS Sports
description: Carson Beck would get the start if Minshew is sidelined
body:
Carson Beck would get the start if Minshew is sidelined

        The Arizona Cardinals offensive injuries continue to pile up. Shortly after head coach Mike LaFleur announced wide receiver Michael Wilson would be ruled out for the year with a neck injury and added there was a chance Gardner Minshew misses Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Rams, reports came out that the quarterback is feared to have suffered a torn UCL in his throwing arm.According to NFL Network, Minshew could be out for the season and face "months of rehab," pending further testing. Minshew reportedly suffered the injury before halftime but played through it in last week's 17-3 loss against the Seattle Seahawks. If Minshew is sidelined, Carson Beck would be the next man up. Beck would be the third quarterback to start for the Cardinals this season. Jacoby Brissett began the year as their starter before being benched and traded to the Baltimore Ravens earlier this month. Beck was drafted in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft at No. 65 overall. The two-time College Football Playoff national champion has yet to make an appearance in the NFL. He would be the third rookie quarterback to start a game this season, joining Tampa Bay Buccaneers undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels and Washington Commanders seventh-rounder Athan Kaliakmanis. The 24-year-old spent five years at Georgia and his last collegiate season with Miami (FL). He finished with 338 completions, a conference high, for 3,813 yards, 30 touchdowns and 12 interceptions last season. His 72.4 completion percentage was also a conference high.
In 55 total college games, he had 966 completions for 11,725 yards, 88 touchdowns and 32 interceptions. After Brissett's eight games, the team made a change at QB during the third quarter of their Nov. 1 game against the Cowboys, putting in Minshew. Beck was promoted to backup quarterback, with Brissett demoted to the third-string QB shortly before his exit from Arizona.Minshew played two games, with a 71.7 completion percentage, 354 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions, going 0-1 in starts.
The Cardinals currently sit at 3-6 and are in fourth place in the NFC West.

        The Arizona Cardinals will be without their top wide receiver for the rest of the 2026 season. Wideout Michael Wilson will be out for the year with a fracture in his neck, head coach Mike LaFleur announced on Monday.Wilson suffered the injury on the fourth play of the game, but he played through the injury. "He said he kinda had a kink in his neck, but he's such a warrior he didn't think much of it. When the adrenaline wore down and he got his test today, that's when we knew," LaFleur said.  Despite the injury, Wilson still had with the most receiving yards on the team in their Week 9 17-3 loss to the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, finishing with six receptions for 60 yards. This season, he leads the team among wide receivers with 51 receptions on 88 targets for 546 yards and two touchdowns through nine games, all of which were starts. 
The Cardinals have already taken numerous hits to the wide receiver room. Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded earlier this season, Kendrick Bourne is out for the year, and Jalen Brooks is also on IR. With Wilson out, the team will need to rely on undrafted rookie Harrison Wallace III, rookie fifth rounder Reggie Virgil and veteran Simi Fehoko.Wallace has one game played, no starts and no targets this season. Virgil has nine receptions for 54 yards and Fehoko has one reception for 17 yards. In total, all three combine for 71 yards on the season, about 13 percent of what Wilson has alone this year. Fehoko, a six-year veteran, only has 11 receptions across his entire career. Wilson is coming off a career-best 2025 with his first 1,000-yard showing. He finished the year with 1,006 yards on 78 receptions with seven touchdown receptions. The 2023 third rounder has 47 total starts over 55 games, all with the Cardinals, for 2,665 yards on 214 receptions and 16 trips to the end zone. 
CBS Sports Senior Fantasy writer Heath Cummings noted that the injury could have major fantasy football implications as league close in on playoffs. Trey McBride is still expected to see a third of the Cardinals' targets, which makes him a "must-start," but his efficency might dip now that teams have no other pass catchers to worry about.LaFleur added Gardner Minshew could miss Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Rams, as the team fears that Minshew suffered a torn UCL, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. Minshew is getting more tests, but the injury (that Minshew suffered before halftime but played with) could also put him on season-ending IR. Carson Beck taking over would also impact the team's wide receiver production in a negative way. If Zonovan Knight returns, Cummings could see him as a high-end flex in the right matchup, as could Tyler Allgeier if Knight misses more time. Cummings warns to "avoid all Cardinals not named McBride."
